name: Cefuroxime Axetil
sections: White to almost white amorphous powder (axetil), slightly soluble in water.

A second-generation cephalosporin on the WHO List of Essential Medicines; widely used for respiratory tract and Lyme disease infections. First approval/introduction: Patented 1971; approved 1977 (Glaxo); oral axetil 1987.

Prodrug hydrolysed to cefuroxime; binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis (bactericidal). Stable to many beta-lactamases; active against Streptococci, Staphylococci (MSSA), H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, E. coli, Klebsiella. Receptor / target profile: Bactericidal: binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits peptidoglycan cross-linking; stable to many beta-lactamases.
Axetil ester hydrolysed in intestinal mucosa and blood to cefuroxime; cefuroxime not metabolised
Summary: Bioavailability ~37% fasting, ~52% with food (take after meals). Tmax 2–3 h. ~50% protein bound. Excreted unchanged in urine. Half-life 1.2–1.5 h.
Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, community-acquired pneumonia (step-down)
Adults: 250–500 mg twice daily after food for 5–10 days
Early Lyme disease: 500 mg twice daily for 20 days
Children (≥3 months): 10–15 mg/kg twice daily (max 500 mg/day)
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
History of immediate severe hypersensitivity to any beta-lactam
Take after food (improves absorption); tablets have bitter taste – do not crush.
Cerebral irritation, convulsions; haemodialysis removes cefuroxime.
Nadelman et al., Ann Intern Med 1992 – cefuroxime axetil as effective as doxycycline in early Lyme disease.
Effective in sinusitis, otitis media and AECB trials.
Report severe diarrhoea, rash or breathing difficulty
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
